paragraphs: Humans are not created as puppets merely following instructions; instead, they receive from the creator the gift of free will, through which countless possibilities, good and bad, can become reality. Even life’s ultimate purpose and mission can be embraced or rejected. Yet every action carries consequences: freedom to act does not mean freedom to undo what follows. Thus free will is a dangerous gift. Fortunately, the creator also gives humanity intelligence: the ability to learn from experience, gain knowledge, and grow in understanding. With these gifts comes the responsibility to cultivate wisdom through reflection and self-correction, and to exercise freedom in ways that honor the divine likeness in oneself and others.

Influential thinkers illuminate different aspects of these gifts. Augustine holds that free will is a good that makes righteous living possible, even though it can be misused to turn away from the good [33]. Aquinas grounds free choice in rational deliberation: humans can compare alternatives and judge what to pursue or avoid, rather than act only through instinct [34]. Aristotle teaches that choosing wisely requires practical judgment informed by experience. We are responsible for our freely chosen actions and cannot always undo their effects simply by changing our minds [32]. From the East, the Book of Odes (Shijing) urges us to govern our conduct with care [35]. Confucius likewise joins learning with reflection and presents lifelong moral cultivation as the path to becoming a junzi, a person of wisdom and moral integrity [36].

Free will allows humans to choose their course; intelligence enables them to learn how to choose wisely. Together, these gifts enable us to embrace our calling and pursue a meaningful and joyful life pleasing to God. Freedom, when exercised responsibly, can bring good to ourselves, our families, our communities, and the entire world, making each a welcoming dwelling place for God.
